correctness.rationale: For every odd prime power \(q\), the quadratic étale norm-one algebra has cyclic unit torus of order \(n=q-\chi_q(-1)\). Additive Fourier inversion identifies the kernel of a directional Fourier slice with vanishing line-fibre sums. Nonisotropic fibres are exactly one- or two-point orbits of \(R_u(z)=a_u z^{-1}\), so two slices impose invariance under the rotation \(r=a_v a_u^{-1}\) and antisymmetry under one reflection. On the cyclic quotient of order \(h=n/\operatorname{ord}(r)\), the fixed-point equation \(w^2=a_u\) has one solution if \(h\) is odd, two if \(h\) is even and \(\chi_q(Q(u))=1\), otherwise none. The number of two-cycles is the entire kernel dimension, and their signed coset indicators form a basis. Nonisotropic directions biject with the norm-one torus; orders \(n\) or \(n/2\) (with the square-norm condition) give the stated totient count. In the split case, each isotropic projection is separately injective. Exact modular line-incidence ranks over ten fields, including three quadratic extensions, independently match all 1,914 tested nonisotropic direction pairs and every isotropic single-view test. The unrestricted result follows from the group-theoretic proof, not the finite tests.

value.rationale: Unit norm conics are canonical split/nonsplit homogeneous finite-field curves, and Fourier line measurements are a natural sparse-angle tomography model. The theorem identifies every kernel and every injective pair, a totient-valued global count, and a sharp one-view/two-view dichotomy caused by isotropic projective directions, with an explicit geometric mechanism and all kernel modes. These invariants are naturally motivated by conic inverse recovery; they are not arbitrary small finite instances, a trivial Fourier normalization, or a claim of noisy reconstruction stability. No general downstream theorem is needed for the exact complete classification to have independent mathematical value.
